item.source_title: Susan Sontag, On Photography (Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Picador; essays 1973-77, book 1977)
item.source_locator: "The Heroism of Vision", the passage beginning "The painter constructs, the photographer discloses" (spine 8)
item.question: You are asked to judge a tightly cropped photograph in which the subject is not identifiable — it reads as an abstract form. On Sontag's account, what has to happen before any judgement is possible, and what does that imply about the standing of formal qualities in photography?
item.answer: On her account the subject has to be identified first, and until it is, the judgement cannot be made at all. Her evidence is exactly this case: a photograph seen too closely or too distantly cannot be reacted to at all until the viewer knows what piece of the world it is. Two cases carry it. A photographed cabbage leaf reads as a fall of gathered cloth and needs a title to identify it — and the image then works in two ways, the form pleases and it is, surprisingly, a cabbage leaf, where gathered cloth would not have been beautiful because that beauty is already known from the fine arts. And a shape resembling a bare coronet becomes far more interesting once one learns it is a splash of milk. Her conclusion: the painter constructs and the photographer discloses, so the formal qualities of style — the central issue in painting — are at most of secondary importance in photography, while what a photograph is of is always of primary importance.
item.support: The Heroism of Vision: the identification of the subject of a photograph always dominates our perception of it, as it does not necessarily in a painting; the painter constructs, the photographer discloses; the subject of the cabbage-leaf photograph looks like gathered cloth and a title is needed; if it were gathered cloth it wouldn't be so beautiful; what looks like a bare coronet becomes far more interesting when we find out it is a splash of milk.
confounders: reading it as advice about titling or captioning images; she is describing how they are processed
assuming she is dismissing composition; her claim is about the order in which the two questions are asked

item.claim: Sontag states a difference in how the two kinds of image are processed. The identification of a photograph's subject always dominates our perception of it, in a way that is not necessarily true of a painting — the painter constructs, the photographer discloses. Her evidence is what happens with a visually ambiguous image: a photograph seen too closely or too distantly cannot be reacted to at all until the viewer knows what piece of the world it is. Two named cases carry the argument. A photographed cabbage leaf that looks like gathered cloth needs a title to identify it, and the image then works in two ways — the form pleases, and it is, surprisingly, a cabbage leaf — where gathered cloth would not have been beautiful, because that beauty is already known from the fine arts. And a shape resembling a bare coronet becomes far more interesting on learning it is a splash of milk. Her conclusion is that the formal qualities of style, the central issue in painting, are at most secondary in photography, while what a photograph is of is always primary.

mechanism.text: Because a photograph is received as a piece of the world, the question "what is this?" runs before any question about how it looks, and the answer supplies the terms in which the looking is then done. A painting carries no equivalent prior question, so form can be primary.

scope.conditions: images received as photographs, particularly close-up or abstracting ones

caveats.text: Argued from two celebrated images and a general observation about ambiguity, not from any systematic comparison. It is a claim about how photographs are looked at, offered by a critic looking at them.
This lane records it as a claim about reading, not about making. Sontag prescribes nothing here and nothing is inferred about how any image should be composed.

positive.description: a photographed cabbage leaf that reads as gathered cloth until it is titled, whose beauty she argues depends on the identification
a high-speed photograph resembling a bare coronet, said to become far more interesting once it is known to be a splash of milk

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', section 'Secondary Opaque Subjects'
item.question: A labelled glass bottle has to look premium and its label has to be legible. The lighting that gives the bottle its describing highlight puts a sheen across the paper. Work through the book's options and say which it rules out and why.
item.answer: The conflict is real and the book states it: most of a paper's reflection is diffuse but some is direct, so the light producing the direct reflection on the glass is also likely to obscure the label. Two remedies work. Move the offending light higher, so the label's direct reflection goes downward instead of toward the lens. Or, where good highlight placement forbids moving the light, interpose a small opaque card blocking exactly the angles that produce direct reflection on the label — and its size is critical: a gobo extending beyond the label's own family of angles will itself reflect in the glass. A polarizing filter is the third option and the book rules it out in most cases: much of the desirable highlight on the glass is usually polarized already, so a polarizer that eliminates the label's reflection is also likely to interfere with the light the glass needs. Underneath all three sits the prior question the authors insist comes first — which of the two is the principal subject — and they say that cannot be settled on a technical basis at all.
item.support: Ch. 7, 'Secondary Opaque Subjects' for the three options and the gobo size constraint; 'Recognizing the Principal Subject' for the prior decision.
confounders: reaching for the polarizer first, which is the intuitive move and the one the source blocks here
oversizing the gobo, which converts a label fix into a black reflection in the glass
treating this as a legibility defect rather than as a scene lit for the wrong principal subject

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Revealing Shape and Contour', section 'How Much Tonal Variation is Ideal?'
item.question: Why does the book say a simple cube can be lit with a black shadow and a white highlight while a product package usually cannot, and what does it refuse to give you?
item.answer: Because of where the detail is. A simple cube with no important detail on any of its sides can take the full range — the shadow can go black and the highlight white. A package that has to sell a product may have important detail on all three visible sides, and detail in either extreme would be lost, so the highlight must be only slightly brighter and the shadow only slightly darker than the third side. The depth clue is deliberately weakened in exchange for legibility. What the authors refuse to give is a number: they say they never specify lighting ratios in the book because the decision has to be based on the specific subject as well as personal taste. Their stated ideal — a highlight side, a shadow side and a side between — is offered as a standard for evaluating whatever lighting exists, not as a requirement good lighting must meet.
item.support: Ch. 5, 'How Much Tonal Variation is Ideal?', which states both the refusal and the package case in the same short section.
confounders: supplying a ratio anyway; the source's position is that it will not
treating the highlight/shadow/mid ideal as a rule rather than as an evaluation standard

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', sections 'Bright-field Lighting' and 'Dark-field Lighting'
item.question: Define bright-field and dark-field lighting as this book defines them, in terms of the family of angles rather than in terms of the resulting picture.
item.answer: Both are defined by what occupies the two extreme limits of the family of angles that acts on a glass edge — the points the book labels L. Bright-field lighting requires that there be NO light at those limits, so the edge stays dark, and the glass must therefore be shown against a bright background; the authors also call it the dark-on-light approach. Dark-field lighting requires that light come from those limits and from nowhere else, so the edge is bright, and the glass must be shown against a dark background; the light-on-dark approach. The two are the same geometric fact read in opposite directions, which is why the authors call them two attractive opposites.
item.support: Ch. 7, 'Two Attractive Opposites' onward. The L-limits framing is the source's own; the two step sequences give the practical form.

assuming dark-field means less light overall; it uses one very large source

item.source_title: David Airey, Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities (New Riders, 2010)
item.question: A twelve-year-old regional food brand asks for a fresh identity. Its packaging is dated, but shoppers find it on the shelf by one distinctive device. Using Airey's Chapter 5 reasoning, what do you recommend and what is the specific failure you are avoiding?
item.answer: You recommend refinement, not replacement — his stated condition is exactly this pair: the identity has become somewhat dated over recent years, but consumer familiarity with it is high. A complete redesign would be going a step too far when a few adjustments would do while keeping the equity behind the visual intact, and his JCJ case shows the shape of it: change the typeface, keep the distinctive red lettering, and the equity around the old design survives. The specific failure you are avoiding is the Tropicana one: consumers were used to the "straw stuck in an orange" device and brand-loyal customers could easily spot the packaging when shopping; the redesign removed it, and he reports sales of the line falling 20 per cent in less than two months and the company reverting to the old packaging. Before designing anything, he would have you establish the client's actual reasons for rebranding, and ask early whether any focus groups have been run — if not, suggest that questioning existing and potential customers about brand perception should be the first order of business. State the reported outcome as this source's claim: it is cited to trade press, with no controls.
item.support: Printed pp. 63-65 (Tropicana), pp. 67-68 (focus groups), pp. 72-73 (refinement and JCJ). The Tropicana and JCJ pages were rendered and inspected during extraction.
confounders: recommending a full redesign because the identity is dated, which uses only half his condition

item.source_locator: Ch. 4, section 'The Cultural Construction of Meaning', printed pp. 193-194
item.question: What contrast does the source draw between Indian and contemporary Western posters, and what reason does it give for the Indian side of it?
item.answer: Western posters present a dramatic enigma — provocative images and text giving incomplete or paradoxical information — which the public must see the film to resolve, and they are supported substantially by text, including review quotations that function as 'the media seal of approval' plus studio, producer and director credits signalling the film's status. Indian posters 'rarely use text'. The reason given is distribution: with the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, 'text is seen as a cultural barrier' — text picks a language, and picking a language cuts the audience. From the 1980s it has been more common for only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director to appear, printed solely in English, because to the public those three figures are themselves a marker of the style, content and quality of the film.

item.claim: Patel states a structural contrast between two poster traditions. Contemporary Western posters present a dramatic enigma — provocative images and text giving incomplete or paradoxical information — which requires the public to see the film to resolve it, and they are supported substantially by text, including review quotations that function as "the media seal of approval," plus studio, producer and director credits that signal the film's status. Indian posters, in contrast, "rarely use text": with the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, "text is seen as a cultural barrier." From the 1980s onward it has been more common for only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director to appear, printed solely in English, because to the public those three figures are a marker of the style, content and quality of the film. Indian posters accordingly "convey the familiarity of the form and content of the Indian film" rather than an enigma.

mechanism.text: Text has to be read in a language, so any text narrows the poster's reach across a multilingual distribution territory. Where the distribution is wide and the audience already knows the form, the poster's job shifts from posing a question to confirming a familiar promise, and that job can be done by images and by three names.

scope.conditions: Indian film posters from the 1980s onward against contemporary Western practice. Patel notes the earlier Indian convention was different — title and star names prominently in English with Hindi and Urdu titles in smaller lettering nearby — so this too is dated.

item.source_locator: Ch. 4, section 'The Cultural Construction of Meaning', printed pp. 193-194
item.question: A distributor must design one key art for a film releasing simultaneously in six Indian language markets and in three diaspora territories. What does this source's account of text actually argue, and where does the argument stop being about India in 2002?
item.answer: The argument is not that posters look better without text; it is that TEXT PICKS A LANGUAGE AND PICKING A LANGUAGE CUTS THE AUDIENCE. With the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, 'text is seen as a cultural barrier', which is why Indian posters 'rarely use text' while contemporary Western posters carry substantial copy including review quotations acting as 'the media seal of approval'. So the reasoning transfers exactly to the case described: one artwork across nine markets is precisely the condition the convention was a response to, and every word added narrows it. What the source also supplies is what replaced the text — from the 1980s only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director, printed solely in English, because to the public those three names themselves signal the style, content and quality of the film. That second half is where the transfer stops. It depends on a star-and-credit system in which those three names carry meaning to that public, which is a fact about Indian audiences in a particular period and not a general property of names. In a diaspora territory whose audience does not hold that system, removing the text removes the signal and does not replace it, and the source says nothing about what would. Nothing here is measured either: no comparison of a text-carrying and a text-free poster is reported anywhere in the book.
item.support: 'text is seen as a cultural barrier'
item.confounders: Treating this as a minimalist design principle inverts it. The convention is a distribution constraint, and in a single-language market the constraint is absent.

item.question: What does this source say changed after economic liberalisation, and why is this the object in the record most likely to be out of date?
item.answer: She describes a double movement: 'one set of processes creates identifiable symbols of cultural identity while another lays down the universal ground within which these markers of difference operate.' The mechanism she names in the trade is concrete — 'advertising agencies in India — the new Ravi Varmas, if you will — often use proprietary analytical models from their parent companies overseas, filling in the blanks with content specific to Indian market segments.' With it comes a narrowing of what 'culture' is taken to mean: circumscribed, globally portable signs of heterogeneity — language, dress, food, music, art, rituals, festivals — grafted onto the protocols of a putatively universal modernity, which relegates cultural difference to leisure and harnesses it to niche marketing. IT IS THE MOST DATED OBJECT IN THE RECORD because it is a characterisation of a media landscape observed to roughly 2004-06, drawn largely from one firm's transformation seen at two points, and it precedes the Indian smartphone, cheap mobile data, UPI and streaming entirely — any of which would change the picture materially.
item.support: agencies 'use proprietary analytical models from their parent companies overseas, filling in the blanks with content specific to Indian market segments'
item.confounders: The template-plus-local-content observation is sharp and quotable, which is precisely why its date and its narrow evidence base need to travel with it.

all you can hope to do is explain their virtues more persuasively than your competitors, and to differentiate them by the style of your advertising. This is the 'added value' which advertising contributes
item.claim: Many products are not different from their competitors, because manufacturers share technology and use the same research to set colour, size, design and taste. For such parity products the only available moves are to explain their virtues more persuasively and to differentiate by the style of the advertising. The source calls this the added value advertising contributes.

mechanism.text: Shared technology and shared research methods converge products on the same attributes, leaving no product-level difference to advertise.

scope.conditions: product categories where competing products are materially alike

caveats.text: the author adds that he is not sufficiently puritanical to hate himself for it, marking the practice as one he expects to be criticised

source_stated_problems: so many products are no different from their competitors
source_stated_remedies: explain the product's virtues more persuasively than competitors do
differentiate by the style of the advertising

intra_source_relations.note: rests on image being what consumers experience
the positively good approach is offered as the alternative to claiming superiority

source_terms: Demonstrations which show how well your product performs are above average in their ability to persuade.
Studies conducted by Ogilvy & Mather found that commercials which name competing brands are less believable and more confusing than commercials which don't.
There is a tendency for viewers to come away with the impression that the brand which you disparage is the hero of your commercial.
item.claim: Demonstrations showing how well the product performs are above average at persuading, and the source insists they need not be dull, instancing a paperboard bridge driven over by a truck and a glue commercial in which the announcer delivers his pitch hanging upside down by his shoes. He then states a specific and counter-intuitive failure of comparative demonstration: commercials naming competing brands were found less believable and more confusing, and viewers tend to come away with the impression that the disparaged brand is the hero. He notes the practice is illegal in Germany and encouraged by the United States government as consumer information.

mechanism.text: A named competitor is a second brand present in the commercial, and the viewer's memory does not reliably keep the roles straight, so attention paid to the rival can attach to the rival.

scope.conditions: comparative demonstration in commercials; regulatory position stated for 1983

caveats.text: the studies are the source's own agency's and are cited without design, sample, date or effect size

the business-to-business chapter states the opposite emphasis, that demonstrations are most effective when they compare the product's performance with competitors'; the source does not reconcile the two, and the difference may be that the business-to-business case does not require naming
the regulatory facts are those of 1983 in two named countries

source_stated_problems: viewers come away with the impression that the brand which you disparage is the hero
source_stated_remedies: think twice before identifying the competitor by name

positive.description: a paperboard bridge spanning a canyon and driven over by a heavy truck, as a demonstration of strength

intra_source_relations.note: the business-to-business chapter urges comparative demonstration
the same displacement failure as the analogy and the celebrity
